claims.text: Sliding abrasion removes the protective oxide film at lamellar phase boundaries.
Exposed lamellar phases in the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloy have different electrochemical potentials and form localized micro-galvanic cells.
Micro-galvanic coupling accelerates localized corrosion and selective dissolution at interphase boundaries.
Corrosion-induced weakening of interphase boundaries promotes further wear.
The reciprocal promotion of corrosion and wear creates a synergistic feedback loop that accelerates overall material loss.
The initial AlCoCrFeNi alloy is eutectic and contains distinct lamellar phases.
The lamellar phases of the initial alloy are galvanically active.
An intact passive oxide film provides corrosion resistance to the alloy under static conditions at approximately 150°C.
Elevated temperature destabilizes the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in a chloride-containing acidic solution.
Simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion will produce higher localized corrosion current densities at phase boundaries than static immersion.
Simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion will produce deeper and wider wear tracks than static immersion.
Simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion will produce greater total material loss than static immersion.
Total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion will exceed the sum of degradation from wear and corrosion acting separately.
During static immersion at 150°C, the oxide film will remain largely unperturbed and preserve passive protection at lamellar interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies when wear primarily removes oxide rather than causing substantial bulk deformation.
